title: The Dickinson Oration
subtitle: Independence Day, 1886
intro: In the summer of 1886 a twenty-seven-year-old New York ranchman rode a freight train thirty-five miles to give a Fourth of July speech in a Dakota town six years old. Seven hundred people heard it. One of them told him afterwards he would be president. Eleven questions on the best Independence Day in North Dakota history.
heroCredit: Dickinson, N.D., 1883. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

badge.title: The Dickinson Oration
badge.shareText: I scored {score}/{total} on the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library's Fourth of July quiz — {tier}. Try it:

questions.prompt: Where did Roosevelt give his Fourth of July oration in 1886?
options: Dickinson, Dakota Territory
Medora, the town nearest his ranches
Fargo, on the eastern edge of the territory
Bismarck, the territorial capital
questions.explanation: Dickinson — thirty-five miles east of Medora and six years old at the time. It was the town's first Independence Day celebration, and about seven hundred people turned out, the largest crowd Dickinson had ever assembled. The country was a hundred and ten years old; the town was younger than the ranch Roosevelt was running.
questions.credit: Dickinson, N.D., 1883. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: How did he travel there that morning?
options: In the Marquis de Mores's private carriage
By stagecoach from Medora
On horseback across the buttes
On a freight train up the Northern Pacific line
questions.explanation: A freight train, thirty-five miles from Medora, in company with Arthur Packard — twenty-four years old and editor of the Bad Lands Cow Boy. Neither man knew it, but both were near the end of their time in Dakota, and both would make their reputations in the East.
questions.imageAlt: Medora in 1883, showing the office and company store of the Marquis de Mores
questions.credit: Medora in 1883: the office and company store of the Marquis de Mores. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

options: The Northern Pacific Railroad's local agent
Dr. Victor Hugo Stickney
Joe Ferris, who kept the store in Medora
The Marquis de Mores, who founded Medora
questions.explanation: Stickney, the town physician — the doctor who had patched up Roosevelt's feet that April after a long ride in wet boots, and who vouched for the young New Yorker in front of the crowd. He was among those who remembered the earnestness of the speech for the rest of his life.
questions.credit: Theodore Roosevelt in 1885. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: Who read the Declaration of Independence aloud that day?
options: The schoolmistress, from the platform steps
Roosevelt himself, before his own oration
Western Starr, the justice of the peace
Nobody — the programme left it out that year
questions.explanation: Western Starr, justice of the peace, who read it "in a clear, forcible tone." That was his real name. The programme also included the Dickinson Silver Cornet Band, a wagon of little girls in white dresses representing the states, a display of the newest farm machinery, and a troupe called the Invincibles in masks and grotesque costume.
questions.imageAlt: The town of Dickinson, Dakota Territory
questions.credit: Dickinson, N.D., 1883. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: According to a witness, what did Roosevelt sound like?
options: His voice was pitched somewhere between a squeak and a shriek
He read flatly from a prepared text
So quiet that nobody could hear him
A booming baritone that carried to the back of the crowd
questions.explanation: A witness said he was plainly embarrassed and spoke in a high key, reckoning it somewhere between a "squeak and a shriek." The voice was a lifelong problem and he never entirely solved it. What carried was the earnestness — that, everyone agreed on.
questions.imageAlt: Theodore Roosevelt mounted in ranch clothes
questions.credit: Theodore Roosevelt in ranch costume. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: How did he place himself in relation to his audience?
options: He avoided the question entirely
As one of them — a Westerner as much as an Easterner
As a future candidate for territorial office
As a visiting dignitary from New York
questions.explanation: Twice. "We, grangers and cowboys alike, have opened a new land; and we are the pioneers," he told them — and later, more soberly, "I am, myself, at heart as much a Westerner as an Easterner; I am proud, indeed, to be considered one of yourselves." Whether the permanent residents of Dakota Territory agreed is another matter. He had been there three years.
questions.imageAlt: A roundup herd in the Dakota Badlands
questions.credit: Roundup herd, Dakota Badlands. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University. Publisher's mount and caption strip removed.

questions.prompt: What was the theme of the speech?
options: The blessings and gifts of America
The closing of the frontier
Duty
The cattle business
questions.explanation: Not celebration — duty. The orator before him had offered patriotic boilerplate about a country bounded on the north by the Aurora Borealis and on the west by the Day of Judgment. Roosevelt got up and told the crowd that being a citizen was work. One listener called it more a sermon than a Fourth of July oration.
questions.credit: Theodore Roosevelt in 1885. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: What did he tell the people of Dickinson they were?
options: Pioneers first and citizens second
Subjects of a young republic
Guests on the land
Sovereigns, not subjects
questions.explanation: Sovereigns, not subjects — and then, having flattered them, he turned it round: sovereigns carry the responsibility of governing themselves with wisdom and integrity. It is the argument he would still be making thirty years later, in almost the same words.
questions.imageAlt: The Little Missouri River near Medora
questions.credit: The Little Missouri River, probably near Medora, N.D. Photograph by Theodore Roosevelt. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: What did he say about immigration?
options: The subject had no place in a Fourth of July speech
Every honest immigrant was welcome, whatever his creed
Immigration to the territory ought to be slowed for a decade
Only immigrants with capital enough to ranch should be admitted
questions.explanation: The full sentence matters more than the fragment: "All American citizens, whether born here or elsewhere, whether of one creed or another, stand on the same footing; we welcome every honest immigrant no matter from what country he comes, provided only that he leaves off his former nationality, and remains neither Celt nor Saxon, neither Frenchman nor German, but becomes an American." This is the earliest form of an argument he pressed for the rest of his life, against what he later called hyphenated Americans. It drew both admiration and objection in his own time, and still does.
questions.credit: Dickinson, N.D., 1883. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Who rode back to Medora with him that afternoon?
options: He travelled back alone on the evening train
Sylvane Ferris, one of his Maltese Cross partners
Bill Sewall, his Maine guide and Elkhorn foreman
Arthur Packard, the newspaper editor
questions.explanation: Packard, editor of the Bad Lands Cow Boy, who ran the Badlands' only newspaper out of a one-room office in Medora. He used the train ride to ask Roosevelt what he meant to do with himself, and got a straight answer: better work in a public and political way than in any other.
questions.imageAlt: The office of the Bad Lands Cow Boy newspaper in Medora
questions.credit: Office of the Bad Lands Cow Boy, probably showing Arthur T. Packard and his wife. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

options: That Roosevelt would become President of the United States
That he should stand for Congress from the territory
That New York would eat him alive
That he would never leave Dakota
questions.explanation: By Packard's own account, told years afterwards: he said it outright, and Roosevelt was not in the least surprised — he had clearly reached the same conclusion himself. The only reply Packard remembered was "If your prophecy comes true, I will do my part to make a good one." Fifteen years later, a bullet in Buffalo made it true.
questions.imageAlt: The Bad Lands Cow Boy newspaper office
questions.credit: Office of the Bad Lands Cow Boy, probably showing Arthur T. Packard and his wife. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.
